title: Beyond the Coverage Number: 7 Advanced DFT Concepts Few Engineers Talk About
description: Defect-level math, small delay defects, scan as an attack surface, IJTAG, packetized scan, silent data corruption and the fall of IDDQ.
content:
A chip can report 99% fault coverage and still fail in a customer's data center. The gap between those two facts is where advanced DFT lives.

This post skips the basics of scan insertion and ATPG. It covers seven ideas that shape how modern silicon is tested, and which rarely come up outside experienced DFT teams.

> "Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence."
>
> — Edsger W. Dijkstra

Dijkstra was talking about software, but the same limit applies to silicon. Every concept below is a way of shrinking the gap between what we tested and what we shipped.

---

## 01 — The math that makes the last 1% matter

Coverage is a test metric. Customers care about **defect level**: how many bad parts escape, measured in defective parts per million (DPPM).

The classic Williams–Brown model links the two:

```python
def defect_level_dppm(yield_: float, coverage: float) -> float:
    """Williams-Brown: DL = 1 - Y ** (1 - T)"""
    return (1 - yield_ ** (1 - coverage)) * 1e6
```

At 80% yield, here is what each step of coverage buys:

| Fault coverage | Escapes (DPPM) |
| --- | --- |
| 90% | ~22,000 |
| 95% | ~11,100 |
| 99% | ~2,230 |
| 99.5% | ~1,100 |
| 99.9% | ~220 |

Going from 99% to 99.9% looks like a rounding error on a dashboard. On the shipped product, it cuts escapes by about **10×**.

> Coverage tells you what you tested. Defect level tells you what you shipped.

---

## 02 — Small delay defects: when "at-speed" is not fast enough

Transition fault ATPG finds *a* path through each fault, and it usually picks the easiest, which is often the shortest. A small extra delay on a short path has plenty of slack to hide in, so the test passes even though the defect is real.

**Timing-aware ATPG** uses static timing data to steer each fault through its **longest** sensitizable path, where a small delay actually breaks the capture. The cost is more patterns; the benefit is catching the subtle resistive defects that later become field failures.

> [!NOTE]
> Small delay defects matter most at advanced nodes, where a resistive via or a slightly thin wire adds tens of picoseconds instead of causing a hard failure.

---

## 03 — Your scan chain is an attack surface

Scan gives full control and visibility of every flop, which is exactly what an attacker wants. Researchers showed back in 2004 that an encryption key could be recovered by running a crypto block in functional mode, switching to scan, and shifting out its internal state.

Common countermeasures:

- **Wipe secrets on mode switch**: clear key registers whenever test mode changes.
- **Lock the test port**: unlock scan only with a challenge–response key.
- **Exclude secret flops** from the chains and test them with on-chip BIST instead.

```verilog
// Clear the key whenever test mode toggles, so secrets never reach scan-out
always @(posedge clk) begin
  test_mode_q <= test_mode;
  if (test_mode ^ test_mode_q) key_reg <= '0;
  else if (key_load)           key_reg <= key_in;
end
```

> The feature that makes a chip testable is the same feature that makes it readable.

---

## 04 — IJTAG: a network that reconfigures itself

A modern SoC holds hundreds of embedded instruments: temperature sensors, PLL controls, memory BIST engines, voltage monitors. Chaining them all into one long JTAG register would make every access painfully slow.

**IEEE 1687 (IJTAG)** solves this with **Segment Insertion Bits (SIBs)**. Each SIB is a one-bit gate: when closed, its whole sub-network is bypassed; when opened, that segment is spliced into the active path. The scan path length changes on the fly.

Engineers describe the network in ICL and write instrument operations in PDL. The tool *retargets* those operations, working out which SIBs to open and how to reach the instrument from the chip pins:

```tcl
iProc read_temp {} {
  iWrite temp_sensor.enable 0b1
  iApply
  iRead  temp_sensor.data   0x5A
  iApply
}
```

You write the test once at the instrument level, and it keeps working wherever that instrument ends up in the hierarchy.

---

## 05 — Packetized scan: freeing cores from pin limits

In hierarchical test, each core is wrapped (IEEE 1500 style) and tested on its own. The bottleneck becomes the **chip-level pins**: you can only test as many cores in parallel as you have scan channels to give them.

**Packetized scan delivery**, such as Siemens' Streaming Scan Network, sends scan data over a shared, fixed-width bus as packets. Each core picks out the bits addressed to it. This means:

- Core-level patterns stay unchanged when the core is reused in a new chip.
- The number of pins no longer limits how many cores test in parallel.
- Bandwidth is allocated to each core according to how much data it needs.

> [!TIP]
> When planning hierarchical DFT, size the scan bus for total test time across all cores, not for the largest single core.

---

## 06 — Silent data corruption: the defects ATPG never saw

In 2021, Google published *"Cores that don't count"* and Meta published *"Silent Data Corruptions at Scale"*. Both described the same unsettling finding: a small fraction of server CPUs that passed manufacturing test occasionally computed **wrong answers**, without crashing and without raising any error.

These "mercurial cores" often fail only under specific instructions, temperatures, voltages or ages. The response is shifting DFT from a one-time factory step to a **lifecycle** discipline:

- **In-field testing** that runs structural patterns periodically during operation.
- **On-chip monitors** that track path margin and aging over the product's life.
- **Fleet-level screening** that compares results across machines to find the outlier.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> For safety-critical parts (ISO 26262), in-system test at key-on, key-off and periodically during operation is a requirement, not an option.

---

## 07 — Why IDDQ testing faded

IDDQ testing measures the quiescent supply current of a CMOS chip. In older processes, leakage was tiny, so a bridging defect that drew a few extra microamps stood out clearly.

At deep sub-micron nodes, normal leakage grew to milliamps and varies widely from die to die. The defect signal disappeared into that spread. Teams adapted with **delta-IDDQ** (comparing current between test vectors on the same die) and statistical outlier screening, but plain absolute IDDQ is now rare at advanced nodes.

It is a good reminder that every test method is tied to the physics of its era.

---

## The takeaway

| Concept | The question it answers |
| --- | --- |
| Defect level math | How many bad parts are we shipping? |
| Timing-aware ATPG | Are we testing the paths that actually fail? |
| Secure scan | Can test access leak our secrets? |
| IJTAG | How do we reach hundreds of instruments efficiently? |
| Packetized scan | How do we test many cores without more pins? |
| In-field test | What happens after the part leaves the tester? |
| Delta-IDDQ | How do we keep current-based testing useful? |

> A coverage number is where DFT starts, not where it ends.
